steel rate, by considering the initial rate of ₹27,500 per MT as adopted in agreement and 
payments were made accordingly. 
Audit noticed that the initial rate of steel adopted in agreement was less than the steel 
rate as per SoR/IBM. Failure to adopt the rate provided in IBM/SoR in the agreement 
and considering price variation over and above ₹27,500 per MT instead of ₹28,000 per 
MT resulted in excess payment of ₹0.12 crore (as detailed in Appendix-IX).

(b) Excess payment of price variation charges for fuel 
As per agreement condition100 of Package IV, price variation in respect of fuel has to 
be calculated based on the formula101 in cases where variation in cost is beyond five per 
cent over the initial rate. The formula contains four components i.e., ‘PF’ (Fuel Factor), 
‘R’ (Value of work done after excluding Value Added Tax (VAT) and Seigniorage 
charges), F1 (the Cost of petrol per litre on the 15th day of the middle month of the 
quarter in the nearest petrol bunk) and Fo (the cost of petrol per litre in the nearest petrol 
bunk on the last date of submission of bids with five per cent variation, i.e. ‘Initial rate’ 
+ five per cent).  
The Department calculated the ‘PF’and ‘R’ values. ‘F1’ values on the 15th day of every 
month was obtained. Accordingly, price variation bills were sanctioned and paid 
periodically as calculated using the formula. Subsequently, the initial sanctions were 
revised by adopting incorrect ‘R’ value (by deducting VAT at 2.8 per cent instead of 
prevailing four per cent) and “Fo” value in denominator (‘initial rate’ instead of ‘initial 
rate + five per cent’). Accordingly, the Department made additional sanctions102 of 
₹4.50 crore (January 2014: ₹3.95 crore & November 2017: ₹0.55 crore) and difference 
in variation was paid.   
Audit noticed that the ‘R’ value has to be calculated after deducting VAT at four per 
cent instead of 2.8 per cent. Further the ‘Fo’ value in denominator of the formula should 
be adopted as ‘initial rate + five per cent’ instead of ‘initial rate’. This resulted in excess 
payment of ₹2.91 crore towards price variation as detailed in Appendix-X. 
The Government replied (January 2023) that adoption of ‘Fo’ value was correct in view 
of orders issued (November 2021) in this regard103 and admitted the audit objection in 
respect of adoption of VAT percentage and promised to revise the calculations and to 
recover the excess paid amount. 
The reply in respect of adoption of ‘Fo’ value was not correct. As in the above said 
Government Order, it was mentioned (Para No. 7) that instructions given in the order 
are not applicable to works taken up prior to this order and orders issued earlier would 
continue to apply for all ongoing works, as per agreement conditions.

A. Sanction of additional quantities 
(i) As per the original scope of work (Package II), design and execution of structures on 
feeder canal has to be made for Stage II discharge of 328 cumecs (85 cumecs for 
Stage I). The Teegaleru canal has to be excavated for creation of 62,000 acres of 
ayacut. The Department sanctioned additional quantities, in respect of structures on 
feeder canal, by stating that the discharge was increased from 85 to 328 cumecs, and 
supplementary agreements125 for ₹17.03 crore were concluded. Similarly, in 
Teegaleru canal, an amount of ₹20.84 crore was sanctioned towards additional 
quantities of CM & CD works and two supplementary agreements126 were concluded.  
As per provisions of EPC contract, the contractor is not eligible for any additional 
amounts for additional quantities if there is no change in the scope of work. However, 
the Government sanctioned an amount of ₹37.87 crore towards additional quantities 
for the structures on feeder and Teegaleru canal despite there was no change in scope 
of work. 
The Department replied (March 2022) that the execution of feeder canal was 
entrusted with 85 cumecs discharge and subsequently, revised to 328 cumecs. This 
led to change in basic parameters and hence additional quantities were sanctioned 
and accordingly supplemental agreements were concluded. These provisions are 
essentially required to complete the balance work to arrive the intended benefits. 
The reply is not acceptable. The execution of structures on feeder canal has to be 
made for 328 cumecs discharge as per the original scope of work. As such, there was 
no revision in basic parameters. Hence, the recommendation for sanction towards 
additional quantities is against the laid down provisions of EPC contract system. 
(ii) As per the scope of work of Package IV (EMC first reach), designing and execution 
of structures on EMC was to be done for Stage II parameters. The State Level 
Standing Committee (SLSC) recommended (January 2019) an amount of 
₹36.40 crore at agreement rates towards additional quantities by stating increase in 
quantities as per approved designs than provided in the IBM and also due to increase 
in number of structures from 30 (as per estimate) to 49 (as per approved designs). 
Government accorded127 (April 2019) administrative sanction and supplementary 
agreement128 was concluded (August 2019) with the contractor.

The Department admitted (March 2022) that there was decrease in length of canal 
and stated that the works were entrusted under EPC contract system wherein 
contractor has to follow the basic parameters and there may be increase/ decrease in 
lengths and quantities. The payments are being made as per the approved payment 
schedule. Further, stated that the contractor is bound to complete all the components 
of works as per the agreement conditions within the limits of provisions made in the 
approved payment schedule. 
However, the proportionate cost towards reduction in length of canal was not 
recovered. 
C. Savings in Earthwork quantities 
(i) As per original agreement (August 2005) of Link canal, EMC (first reach) and 
Kakarla dam, the contractor141 has to investigate and design these components for 
Stage II. The execution was initially limited to Stage I. Subsequently, the Department 
proposed to execute these items for Stage II. Accordingly, the total quantities was 
assessed for both Stage I and II for Link canal, EMC first reach and Kakarla dam as 
50,11,837 cum, 1,99,73,392 cum and 2,68,138 cum respectively. The execution for 
Stage II was entrusted (January 2009) to same contractor at original agreement rates. 
Out of above total quantities, the quantities as per execution, as stated in status 
reports, work bills etc., towards link canal, EMC 1st reach and Kakarla dam was 
33,05,518 cum, 1,55,00,000 cum and 2,27,600 cum respectively.

initial agreement to December 2012 were not recorded and were not mentioned in the

deviation from the basic parameters and scope of work and payment made were

non recording the quantities upto December 2012 in the status report was not correct.

reduction in earthwork quantities by 0.62 crore cum with a proportionate cost of 
₹60.47 crore143.

turnkey contract system and also the quantities given in Bill of Quantities were meant 
for general assessment of value of work done and these were subject to alterations, 
additions and deductions. The basis for payment would be percentage payment at 
various stages of work which would be assessed on quantities measured by the 
contractor and approved by Engineer-in-Charge to complete the work as per scope of 
work.

recovered.

P R E F A C E 
 
This Report for the year ended March 2021 has been prepared for 
submission to the Governor of Madhya Pradesh  under the 
Comptroller and Auditor General’s (Duties, Powers and 
Conditions of Service) Act, 1971. 
The Report contains significant results of the audit of Panchayat i 
Raj Institutions  and Urban Local Bodies in the State  including 
the Departments concerned. 
The issues noticed in the course of test audit for the period 2019-
21 as well as those issues which came to notice in ear lier years 
but could not be dealt with in  the previous Reports  have also 
been included, wherever necessary. 
The audit has been conducted in conformity with auditing 
standards issued by the Comptroller and Auditor General of 
India. 

  
 
OVERVIEW 
 

 

 
OVERVIEW 
This Report contains five chapters. The first Chapter provides an overview of the 
functioning, accountability mechanism and financial reporting issues  of 
Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs)  and fourth chapter provides an overview of 
functioning o f Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) . The second Chapter contains two 
Performance Audit report s on PRIs. The third and fifth Chapter contain four 
Compliance Audit reports, one  on PRIs  and three on ULBs . A summary of 
important findings is presented in this overview.  
Chapter I: An Overview of the Functioning , Accountability Mechanism and 
Financial Reporting Issues of the Panchayati Raj Institutions 
• Annual Audit Plans of Local Fund Auditor (LFA) for the year 2019-21 were 
forwarded with delay ranged between one  and five months to Principal 
Accountant General (Audit-I) Madhya Pradesh 1. Further, LFA acted only on 
36 IRs Inspection Reports ( IRs), out of 102 IRs of LFA  sent and  vetted in 
office of Principal Accountant General (Audit -I) Madhya Pradesh  during 
2019-21. 
(Paragraph 1.4.1) 
• Despite letters  regarding submission of compliance/ remedial action taken 
against outstanding audit paragraphs  issued to ZPs/JPs, 11,726 paragraphs of 
2,693 IRs of Principal Accountant General  (Audit) were outstanding for 
settlement as of 31st March 2021.  
(Paragraph 1.5) 
• Required number of Social audits were not conducted  (only 36,995 out of 
required 91,236) in GPs  during 2019 -21. Further, 2286 Social Audit  issues  
(` 1.11 crore) of 17 districts remained for settlement. 
(Paragraph 1.6) 
• As per accepted recommendation of 3rd SFC by State Government , Finance 
Department did not devolve  State Finance Commission  (SFC) grants of  
` 2440.73 crore to PRIs during 2019-21.   
(Paragraph 1.7.2) 
• PRIs could not utilise funds allotted by the State Government a nd the saving 
was between 5 and 24 per cent during 2019-21. 
        (Paragraph 1.7.3)

An overview of the functioning of the Panchayati Raj Institutions in the State 
 
1.1   Introduction  
The Constitution (73rdAmendment) Act, 1992 conferred Constitutional status to Panchayats 
and provided inter alia for the creation of Panchayats at village, intermediate and district 
level with, fixed tenure and regular election, devolution of powers and responsibilities given 
to the Panchayats by the State Legislative Assembly for establishing local self-Government 
system. Consequently, Madhya Pradesh State Legislature enacted the Madhya Prades h 
Panchayat Raj evam Gram Swaraj Adhiniyam , 1993  (called PRI Act hereinafter) to 
establish a three-tier system viz.  Gram Panchayat, Janpad Panchayat and Zila Panchayat at 
Village, Block and District level respectively. There are 51 Zila Panchayats  (ZPs), 3 13 
Janpad Panchayats (JPs) and 22809 Gram Panchayats (GPs) in the State as of March 2021.

1.3   Functioning of PRIs 
Article 243G of the Constitution of India provides that the Legislature of a State may, by 
law, endow Panchayats with such powers and authority as may be necessary to enable 
them to functi on as institutions of self -government and such law may contain provisions 
for the devolution of powers and responsibilities upon Panchayats.  
1.3.1   In terms of PRI Act, every ZP shall consist of elected members, who are 
empowered to elect a President and  a Vice -President. The President is responsible for 
acting on the resolutions of the ZP, and following the directions of the State Government 
for ensuring proper maintenance of records and registers, authorizing payments, issuing of 
cheques and sanctioning  of refunds etc. The PRI Act also provides for a CEO and one or 
more Additional CEO at ZP level appointed by the State Government.  
ZPs are responsible to prepare annual plans for economic development and social justice of 
the district and ensure the coordinated implementation of such plans. It shall ensure overall 
supervision, co-ordination and consolidation of the plans prepared by JPs and reallocate to 
JPs and GPs the funds made available by Central or State Government. 
1.3.2   Janpad Panchayats (JPs) are the intermediate tier of PRIs at Block level .  Every JP 
has elected members, President and a Vice -President. President of JP has similar power 
and responsibility as President of ZP enjoys. As per s ection 69(2) o f PRI Act, State 
Government shall appoint C EO and  one or more  Additional CEOs for JPs . CEO of  JP 
controls and supervises the administration of community development block and tribal 
development block within its jurisdiction. The function and schemes assigned to such 
block by the State Government are implemented under the superintendence, directions, and 
control of JP in accordance with the instructions issued by the State Government from time 
to time. 
Further, under section 50 of PRI Act, JPs are also responsible to consider and consolidate 
the annu al plan  of GPs  in respect of economic development and social justice and to 
submit the consolidated plan to ZP. 
1.3.3   Gram Panchayats (GPs) the last tier of PRIs at the grassroot level of PRIs, consist of 
elected Panch and Sarpanch who implements the res olutions of the GP and follow the 
directions of the State Government. GPs  are responsible to ensure execution of schemes, 
works, projects entrusted  to them by any law and those assigned to them by Central or 
State Government or ZP or JP. According to Secti on 49-A of PRI Act, it shall be the duty

2.1   Implementation of 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act 
 
Executive Summary 
Government of India (GoI) enacted the 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act (73rd CAA), 
1992 (came int o effect from April 1993) to strengthen the local self -government at 
Panchayats. The main features of 73rd CAA are to establish three-tier structure panchayat 
at village, block and district level; constitution of State Election Commissi on for regular 
election in panchayats at every five years; proportionate seat reservation for SC, ST and 
women; constitution of State Finance Commission, Gram Sabha at Gram Panchayat level. 
In addition, constitution of District Planning Committee (DPC) for  comprehensive 
planning of the district.  
Government of Madhya Pradesh (GoMP) enacted the Madhya Pradesh Panchayat Raj 
Evam Gram Swaraj Adhiniyam, 1993 (called hereinafter PRI Act) came into existence 
from January 1994 to accord constitutional status to th e Panchayati Raj Ins titutions 
(PRIs), provides constitution of Standing Committee at each PRI level for the preparation 
of budget, annual accounts and development plans; supervisory power to Zila Panchayat 
(ZP) and Janpad Panchayat (JP) and execution al power to Gram Panchayat  (GP) for 
various centrally and state sponsored schemes.  
Further, in view of devolution of 29 functions mentioned in the 11th schedule of Article 
243G of the Constitution to Panchayats, GoMP issued (January 1997) guiding principles 
to the departments for devolution of programme, activities and responsibilities to 
Panchayats.  
The Performance Audit (PA), cover ing the period 2016-21 was conducted by test -check 
of the records of Directorate of four selected departments (apart from Panchaya t Raj 
Directorate) and its district units, 10 ZPs (one ZP from each division), 10 JPs (one JP from 
each selected ZP) and 20 GPs (two GPs from each selected JP) revealed the following:  
• None of the functions, funds and functionaries of test-checked four departments were 
devolved. Further, four departments (other than test -checked departments) took back 
devolved functions, funds and functionaries from PRIs during 1998-2014. 
(Paragraph 2.1.7.1 and 2.1.7.2) 
• GoMP constituted the 3rd, 4th and 5th SFC with a delay of seven months, one and half 
year, and one month 23 days respectively. We also noted that the 3 rd and 4 th SFC 
submitted their reports with a delay of two and half years and four years respectively. 
(Paragraph 2.1.8.1) 
• Despite availability of adequate funds, trainings were not imparted to 70 per cent of 
Elected Representatives (ERs) and 97 per cent of officials, against the target of training 
of 3.92 lakh ERs and 28,150 officials of PRIs.  
(Paragraph 2.1.8.3)

• 35 per cent (71 out of required 200) of DPC meetings were held in selected districts 
during 2016-21. None of the DPCs of selected districts prepared District Development

(Paragraph 2.1.8.4)

2.1.1   Introduction 
To strengthen the local self -government, the Government of India (GoI) enacted the 73rd 
Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992 (73rd CAA) which came into effect from April 1993. 
In view of Article 243G of the Constitution, the Government of Madhya Pradesh (GoMP) 
enacted the 73 rd CAA ( June 1994) and the Madhya Pradesh Panchayat Raj Evam Gram 
Swaraj Adhiniyam, 1993 ( known as PRI Act) came into existence from January 1994  to 
accord constitutional status to the Panchayat i Raj Institutions (PRIs) and made provisions 
for devolution of powers and responsibilities. The 73rd CAA empowers the state Government 
to devolve 29 functions relating 20 departments (Appendix-2.1.1) mentioned in the 11 th 
schedule of Article 243G  in Madhya Pradesh. The various provisions of the 73 rd CAA are 
summarised below: 
• Constitution of Gram Sabha in villages.  
• Constitution of three-tier Panchayat at village, block and district levels.  
• Direct election to all seats of Panchayats. 
• Minimum age for contesting elections to the PRIs be twenty-one years. 
• Reservation of seats for Schedule Castes and Schedule Tribes. 
• Reservation of one-third of the total seats at every level of PRIs for women. 
• Fixing of tenure of five years for Panchayats. 
• Giving representation to the Members of the Parliament, M embers of Legislative 
Assembly (MLAs) and Members of Legislative Council ( MLCs) at the intermediate  
(Block) and district level with full voting rights. 
The PRI Act, 1993 envisages provisions for smooth functioning of Zila Panchayats (ZPs), 
Janpad Panchayats (JPs) and Gram Panchayats (GPs).  At the district level, ZP is entrusted 
with supervisory powers to monitor Janpad Panchayats and Gram Panchayats. The functions 
of JP at Block level are to ensure the execution of schemes, works and projects entrusted to 
it. The functions of GPs at village level a re to prepare socio -economic annual plan and to 
execute various schemes sponsored by GoI and GoMP.  
Besides this, there are provisions for constitution of District Planning Committee (DPC) to 
consolidate the plan prepared by the Panchayats for overall development at district level and 
Standing Committee for preparation of development plans, budget and annual accounts for 
the PRIs.

Madhya Pradesh (MP) located in central India, is the second largest state of the country. The 
area of the State is 3.08 lakh Square km out of which the rural area is 3.00 lakh Square km. 
As per census 2011, 72.31 per cent (5.25 crore) of total population (7.26 crore) reside in 
rural areas of Madhya Pradesh (MP).

under Panchayat and Rural Development Department (PRDD) . The category wise detail is

and ZP/JP/GP (Accounting) Rules, 1999 in PRI Act for maintenance of accounts in PRIs.

recommended budget and accounting formats (eight43) in 2002. Ministry of Panchayati Raj 
and GoMP accepted these accounting formats in 2007 and 2010 respectively for 
implementing in PRIs.

generated by the portal. The web portal also facilitates to generate reports in prescribed eight 
formats and income and expenditure details for monitoring purpose. Further, para 10.111 of 
recommendation of 13 th CFC envisages that , accounts of PRIs were to be maintained in 
prescribed formats.

2.1.14   Conclusion 
We noticed that the  objective of 73 rd CAA and PRI Act to strengthen the PRIs to make 
devolution of power and responsibilities to PRIs to ensure their effective role in 
developmental activities and local self-governance could not be achieved due to following 
reasons:  
(i) None of  the departments transferred functions as envisaged in Article 243G of        
73rd CAA except seven functions already with PRDD. 
(ii) None of the departments transferred functionaries/ officials under the control of PRIs 
even after 27 years.  
(iii) None of the departments transferred their assets to PRIs. 
(iv) In Madhya Pradesh only 30 per cent ERs and three per cent officials were trained 
during 2016-21 despite availability of funds. 
(v) Despite an increase in divisible fund, there was steep decline in devolution of funds 
(2017-18 to 2020 -21) which declined 64  from 4.17 per cent  in 2016 -17 to                     
0.79 per cent of the divisible funds in 2020-21.  
(vi) PRIs did not levy taxes adequately to fulfil their need as provided in the PRI Act. 
(vii) Due to no devolution of functions, funds and functionaries, PRIs had shortage of 
functionaries to collect taxes. 
(viii) The reservation for SC/ST/ Backward and women were adopted, but the participation 
of women in 178 meetings out of 196 meetings was one per cent to 44 per cent only. 
No meeting was conducted with desired quorum.  
(ix) The Gram Panchayats are functional with only two functionaries viz. Panchayat 
Secretary and Rojgar Sahayak only. 
We conclude that the objectives of 73rd Constitutional amendment could not be achieved so 
far as the functions, functionaries and funds were not transferred effectively to the PRIs as 
envisaged in the Act and they could not be transformed into institutions of self-governance 
even after lapse of 27 years since enactment of the Act.

2.2.6.2   Identification and selection of beneficiaries 
Paragraph 4 of framework for implementation of PMAY-G envisaged that identification and 
prioritization of the beneficiaries will be done based on housing deprivation parameters in 
the SECC-2011 data. Priority was to be  assigned based on parameters reflecting housing 
deprivation in each category viz. SC, ST, Minorities and Others in each priority groups (in 
order of Houselessness followed by the number of rooms; Zero, One and Two rooms).  In 
two sub -groups (Automatic Included Households 6 and Other Households ), Automatic 
Included Households shall not rank lower than other households within a priority group. 
Inter-se priority within the two sub -groups will be determined based on their cumulative 
deprivation scores which are calculated from the socio -economic pa rameters with each 
having equal weight. Households with higher deprivation scores will be ranked higher within 
the sub-groups. 
Once the category wise priority lists are generated from SECC data and suitably publicized, 
a Gram Sabha will be convened. The Gram Sabha will verify the fac ts based on which the 
households are identified as eligible. Complaints regarding wrongful deletion/changed 
ranking are examined by an Appellate Committee 7 constituted by the State Government. 
Thereafter, GP wise final PWL for each category will be publish ed on the notice board of 
GP and entered on AwaasSoft.

2.2.6.5(e)  Constitution of PMU 
As per Para 7.3 of PMAY-G Guidelines, a dedicated Programme Management Unit (PMU) 
at State and each ZP/JP level was to undertake the tas k of monitoring and supervision of 
implementation of the scheme. The PMU was to be headed by a full-time programme officer 
or a senior officer at the district level. The other members of District (D) PMU would be 
professionals in the field of construction, IT and Training Coordinator and support staff. The 
duties of DPMU included finalisation of priority list and annual select list, allotment of land 
to the landless beneficiaries, sensitisation of beneficiaries, organisation of training and credit 
linkage and monitoring of reporting on AwaasSoft etc. Similarly, BPMU at block level was 
to be headed by a full -time block level officer or coordinator assisted by technical support 
staff and MIS data entry operator.  BPMU would do registration of beneficiaries, iss ue of 
sanction orders, tagging of trained masons to beneficiaries, monitoring of progress of 
constructions and reporting through AwaasSoft etc.

2.2.7   Conclusion 
State completed 21.64 lakh houses (82.35 per cent) against 26.28 lakhs houses sanctioned 
(as per AwaasSoft) under PMAY-G during 2016-21, however, the timeliness prescribed for 
completion was adhered to in 86.28 per cent of the completed house. 
There was lack of v erification of beneficiarie s in exclusion process as b eneficiaries with 
2/3/4 wheeler vehicles were provided benefit. Further, priority setting and sanction as per 
priority as indicated in guidelines were also not adhered to by the State. 
MGNREGA Job Card of another person was registered on AwaasSoft portal instead of actual 
beneficiary. Aadhaar number of 97.70 per cent  beneficiaries were collected during 
registration but as per MIS only 28.33 per cent were seeded in AwaasSoft in selected Janpad 
Panchayats.  
Timely release of Centre and State share in State Nodal Account was not followed as per 
guidelines by the S tate. Timely release of 1st instalments to sanctioned bene ficiaries was 
done only in 33.47 per cent cases. 
1st inspection of sanctioned houses was done after stipulated time in 40.54 per cent cases 
and it reflects lack of monitoring at different levels. AwaasApp (mobile application) adopted 
for geo-tagging of photographs at different level of construction for monitoring of progress 
was also not accurate. This resulted in the lack of adequate control of AwaasApp in capturing 
geo-reference date and time stamped photographs  of same houses at different construction

3.3.1   Non-submission of UCs by PRIs 
Department directed (De cember 201 6) that release of SFC grant s to the ZPs/JPs was 
subject to utilization of 70 per cent of previous year ’s grant and 100 per cent  of other 
years’ grant.  
Audit noticed that only five9 ZPs/JPs out of 14 selected ZPs/JPs10 submitted total 12 UCs 
out of the required 42 UCs for the year 2017 -20. Panchayat Raj Directorate (PRD) neither 
asked for utilization certificates nor maintain records of funds drawn and utilized by the 
districts. Thus, the Department failed to monitor the utilization of grants by  the ZPs/JPs. 
Consequently, during the year 2018 -20, grants were released to the districts without 
ensuring their utilization. 
Audit further noticed that although the Commissioner ’s office  was required to ensure 
submission of UCs,  it did not maintain the r ecords of utilization of grant . Therefore, the 
Department did not even have the data to enforce the conditions of grant as stipulated by 
the SFC.  
The Government replied (July 2022)  that as per SFC guidelines, grant s were released as 
per budget allotment  without obtaining UCs from the PRIs . However, cent per  cent 
valuation and verification of works being executed from these grants were done. 
Reply is not acceptable  as the department did not comply  with the norms of SFC 
guidelines in releasing the grants to ZPs/JPs.

3.4.3   Execution of works without laboratory testing 
As per instructions issued (February 2018) by PRDD, it was the primary responsibility of 
the executing agenc y and Sub/Assistant Engineer (SE/AE) of Rural Engineering Services 
(RES) Department to execute the quality work and the material as well as works were to be 
tested up to the prescribed frequency to ensure the quality of work.  Further, the rates given 
in the Schedule of Rates (S OR) issued (February 2016) by the RES Department, GoMP, 
were inclusive of the cost of  laboratory testing12 to be conducted as per the  prescribed 
frequency.  
Directorate, PRIs issued (June 2017) order to constitute a monitoring cell to evaluation the 
online & offline activities conducted under various schemes. 
Audit observed that  laboratory tests for ascertaining quality was undertaken in only 20 
works (12 per cent ) out of 163 test checked works . In respect of remaining 143 work s 
(Appendix-3.5) amounting to ` 9.12 crore, quality tests were not conducted. Consequently, 
the manner in which the RES Department evaluated the quality of work without any tests 
could not be ascertained by Audit.  
Government accepted audit observation and  replied (July 2022) that the laboratory testing 
of all works was not possible due to non-availability of lab facilities at all JPs headquarters, 
excess of works and GPs established in remote areas. However, RES ensured the quality of 
works through valuation and verification.

3.4.8 Other irregularities 
3.4.8.1   Issue of Administrative Sanction by incompetent authority 
The Scheme guidelines (August 2016) inter alia stipulate that administrative sanction of 
the work was to be issued by the CEOs of respective ZPs/JPs.  
In ZP Tikamgarh, audit observed that in five17 works pertaining to construction of culverts 
involving expenditure of  ` 32.50 lakh, the concerned GPs issued administrative sanction s 
instead of the CEO, ZP there by violating the provisions of the scheme guidelines. 
CEO, ZP Tikamgarh produced a letter of PRDD (December 2016) and stated that sanctions 
were in order. 
Reply of CEO is not acceptable as the  ibid order envisages th at administrative sanction 
were to be issued by the concerned ZPs and not  by the GPs . The ibid order elaborates 
general financial delegation of power which cannot be applied in special schemes. GPs are 
only implementing agencies. 
The government accepted the facts and stated (July 2022) t hat a letter to investigate the 
matter was issued (June 2022) to the CEOs of respective ZPs. 
3.4.8.2   Issue of improper Technical Sanction 
Engineer-in-Chief of RES issued (March 2017) model estimates for execution of different 
works in PRDD and issued instruction about the thickness of CC roads should be 200 mm. 
Audit o bserved that  in 24 works18 costing ` 1.58 crore , the Technical Sanction for 
construction of CC roads were accorded without mentioning the thickness of roads.  In the 
absence of clear instructions to the executing agencies to provide specific thickness for CC 
roads, the executing agencies were free to construct the roads as per their convenience and 
not as per the set standards.

4.1 Introduction 
The 74th Constitutional Amendment gave constitutional status to Urban Local  Bodies and 
established a system of uniform structure, regular elections and regular flow of funds 
through Finance Commission, etc. As a follow up,  the States are required to entrust these 
bodies with powers, functions and  responsibilities so as to enable them to function as 
institutions of Self-Government. 
Article 243Q of the Constitution envisages that there shall be constituted in  every State, 
Municipal Corporations for large urban areas; Municipal Councils  for smaller urban areas; 
and Nagar Panchayats (by whatever name called)  for areas in transition from a rural to an 
urban area. Further, Article 243W states that the Legislature of a State may, by law, endow 
the Municipalities with  such powers and authority as may be necessary to enable them to 
function as  institutions of Self-Government and such law may contain provisions for 
devolution of powers and responsibilities upon Municipalities. 
There are 16 Municipal Corporations, 9 9 Municipal Councils and 2 92 Nagar Parishads in 
the State as of March 2021. 
4.2 Organisational set up of Urban Local Bodies 
All the Urban Local Bodies are empowered to discharge the functions devolved under the  
provisions of Madhya Pradesh Municipal Corporation Act, 1956 and Madhya  Pradesh 
Municipalities Act, 1961, subject to monitoring powers vested in State Authorities provided 
therein. At the Government level, Urban Development and Housing Department (UDHD) is 
the administrative Department for Urban Local  Bodies. The organisational set up of 
governance of Urban Local Bodies is as under:

4.3 Functioning of Urban Local Bodies 
Article 243W envisaged that the Legislature of a State may, by law, endow the 
Municipalities with such powers and authorities as may be necessary to enable them to 
function as institutions of Self Government and such law may contain provisions for 
devolution of powers and responsibilities upon Municipalities, including 18 functions listed 
in the Twelfth Schedule. The State Government devolved all 18 functions, enshrined in 
Twelfth Schedule of the Constitution  of India  to Urban Local  Bodies, as detailed in 
Appendix-4.1. 
Article 243X of the Constitution of India envisages that State Legislature may, by law, vest 
power in Urban Local  Bodies to impose various taxes for revenue collection. This 
constitutional provision has been incorporated in Clause 132 of Madhya Pradesh Municipal 
Corporation Act, 1956 and Clause 127 of Madhya Pradesh Municipalities Act, 1961. At the 
Urban Local Bodies level various types of taxes have been imposed including Property Tax, 
Composite Tax, Water Tax, Market Fee, etc. 
There are three types of Urban Local Bodies i.e., Municipal Corporation, Municipal Council 
and Nagar Parishad which have been described below: 
• Municipal Corporation 
According to Section 9 of Madhya Pradesh Municipal Corporation Act, 1956, a Municipal 
Corporation shall consist of  a Mayor and Councilors directly elected from the Municipal 
Corporation area. Section 37 of the Madhya Pradesh Municipal Corporation Act, 1956  
provides that there shall be a Mayor-in-Council for every Municipal Corporation constituted 
by the Mayor from amongst the elected Councilors to discharge the functions and conduct 
of business of the Mayor-in-Council, as may be prescribed. 
According to Section 25 of Madhya Pradesh Municipal Corporation Act, 1956, the Mayor 
shall have administrative control over the officers and staff of his office and exercise such 
powers and perform such functions as described in the Act and Rule made thereunder. 
The Commissioner of a Corporation shall be appointed by the State Government who is the 
Principal Executive Officer of the Corporation and shall have the right to speak at, and 
otherwise take part in any meeting of the Corporation or any committee thereof but shall not 
be entitled to vote or to move any proposition. The office of the Commissioner sh all have 
the administrative staff for the functions and duties as prescribed under the rules. The 
Commissioner shall perform all the duties imposed or conferred upon him by this Act and 
exercise supervision and control over the acts and proceedings of all municipal officers. 
• Municipal Council and Nagar Parishad 
As per Section 19 of Madhya Pradesh Municipalities Act, 1961, a Municipal Council, for a 
smaller urban area and Nagar Parishad, for a transitional urban area, shall have a President 
and Councilors elected from the respective areas by direct election. Under Section 70 of the 
Act, there shall be a President -in- Council (PIC) for every Municipal Council/Nagar 
Parishad, which shall be constituted by the President from amongst the elected councilors to 
discharge the functions and conduct of business of the PIC, as may be prescribed. The

President of the Municipal Council/Nagar Parishad, who is the President of PIC, shall 
preside over all meetings, watch over the financial and executive administration and perform 
such executive functions as may be allotted under the Act. 
As per Section 87 of the Act, the Chief Municipal Officer of a Council shall be appointed by 
the State Government, who shall be the Principal Executive Officer of the Municipal 
Council/Nagar Parishad and shall have such powers and perform such functions as described 
in the Act and Rules made thereunder.

4.7  Fourteenth and Fifteenth Finance Commission Grants 
As per 14th (Period 2015 -20) and 15 th (Period 2020 -26) Finance Commission 
recommendations, allocations among various ULBs within the State were to be made by the 
respective States. As per 14th Finance Commission States were required to release the grants 
to the ULBs within fifteen days of it b eing credited to their accounts by the Union 
Government. In case of delay, the State Government must release the instalment along with 
interest at the bank rate of Reserve Bank of India paid from its own funds. Further, as per 
15th Finance Commission States were required to release the grants to the ULBs within ten 
working days of it being credited to their accounts by the Union Government. In case of 
delay, the State Government must release the instalment along with interest for the period of 
delay as per the effective rate of interest on market borrowing/ State Development Loans for 
the previous year. 
Audit scrutiny of information provided by the UADD  for the period 2016 -21 revealed that 
State Government received ` 3,226.33 crore and ` 1,768.50 crore as 14th and 15th Finance 
Commission grant respectively from Government of India (GoI) till March 2021. However, 
the State Government delayed the release of grants to ULBs and the interest of ` 13.77 crore

5.1   Compliance Audit of Smart City Companies of Madhya Pradesh 
 
5.1.1   Introduction 
Cities are engines of growth for the economy of every nation. Nearly 31 per cent of India’s 
population lives in urban areas and contributes 63 per cent of India’s GDP1. With increasing 
urbanization, urban areas are expected to house 40 per cent  of India’s population and 
contribute 75 per cent of India’s GDP by 2030. This requires comprehensive development 
of physical, institutional, social and economic infrastructure. All  these are important in 
improving the quality of life and attracting people and investments to a City, setting in 
motion a cycle of growth and development. The Government of India accordingly introduced 
the “Smart Cities Mission” on 25 th June 2015 for  the Development of Smart Cities. The 
objective was to promote sustainable cities that provide core infrastructure and decent 
quality of life to their citizens including a clean and sustainable environment and application 
of ‘Smart’ Solutions. Though the conceptualisation of Smart C ity varies from city to city , 
depending on the level of development, willingness to change and reform, resources and 
aspirations of the city re sidents; the core infrastructure elements in a Smart City would 
include: 
• adequate water supply, 
• assured electricity supply, 
• sanitation, including solid waste management. 
Smart Cities can be developed either on the lines of the Area Based Development (AB D) 
model or through Pan -city Development (PCD) model.  The strategic components of AB D 
in the Smart Cities Mission are city improvement (retrofitting 2), city renewal 
(redevelopment3) and city extension (greenfield development 4). In case of PCD, some 
components of smart solutions are expected to be provided to all citizens across the city.

consultation with citizens to achieve Smart City objectives to make the existing area more efficient and 
livable. 
3  Redevelopment- Redevelopment envisages an area o f more than 50 acres, identified by Urban Local 
Bodies, in consultation with citizens by replacing the existing built -up environment and enable  
co-creation of a new layout. 
4  Greenfield Development- Greenfield Development is in the vacant area more than 250 acres.

5.1.2   Organisational set-up

Audit noticed that the SCCs in all the four selected Smart Cities had initially engaged citizens

engagement and on the justification that the site was close to the Habibganj (now

made by Bhopal SCC to a new location in North and South Tatya Tope Nagar. The

of the project . However, the approved area of five of the  components were either 
reduced or increased resulting in reduction the total area of the project to 123.34 acres 
without citizen engagement.

Station area was approved comprising of 30 activities. The plan was later revised but 
included 39 activities, and the area was reduced. All the changes were made without

As discussed above, the locations as well as major components/ activities of various projects 
were revised which shows that the Smart City Proposals were prepared without adequate

involved during the process of change in plans. Further, in Bhopal and Indore , the SCC

citizens, while in the case of Ujjain, the land was not available for the earlier planned project,

5.1.5.5   Improper planning for Commercial Complex in Bhopal 
The SCC, Bhopal issued work order (October 2018) for construction of a Commercial 
complex Signature Tower (consisting of one Basement and Ground floor plus eight floors)  
to a contractor at a cost of ` 34.93 crore.  
After the award of the contract, the SCC changed the scope of the work (September 2019) 
by increasing the height of the Complex to 10 floors, and two basements (for parking) so as 
to provide a better monetization model. Estimated cost of the revised projec t was ` 72.73 
crore. The work was to be completed by January 2021. 
After a lapse of 12 months (since changing the scope of work) and a fter incurring 
expenditure of ` 21.06 crore, the project was moving at tardy pace with only the two 
basement floors having  been completed. However, the SCC, instead of penalizing the 
contractor for the shoddy work, decided to sell the Complex in its present stage. The reasons 
for arriving at this decision were not available in the records. The Board in its resolution 
(August 2020) accordingly approved the resolution without seeking reasons for the change 
in plan. Audit observed that: 
• The SCC, Bhopal suffered from complete lack of foresightedness and vision while 
planning for the project. Consequently, after incurring an expenditure of ` 21.06 
crore on building merely two floors, the SCC decided to sell the building which was 
totally illogical and indicated extremely weak planning processes in the SCC. 
• The Board approved the decision without seeking reasons for the same, especially 
since a significant amount had been spent on construction. 
• The SCC , Bhopal  by stopping the work midway (in order to sell t he project) 
indemnified the contractor from paying penalties considering the tardy pace of work 
despite spending almost 36 per cent of the estimate costs. There were no records of 
missed timelines/milestones vis-à-vis the payments processed. 
• After a lapse of 24 months since the stoppage of the work, the SCC, Bhopal is yet to 
sell the under-construction building, which remains in its incomplete condition.

5.1.6.3   Re-ordering to the same supplier instead of calling fresh tenders 
As per clause 22 of Madhya Pradesh Store Purchase rules, 2015, another supply order to the 
same supplier, in continuation of the supply order already placed earlier, may be place d by 
a government agency. But the quantity of the total supply in the new supply order should not 
exceed 50 per cent of the previous order. 
The SCC, Indore had placed an order to M/s Hy va India Pvt. Ltd. (June 2017) for supply, 
erection, and commissioning of Transfer Station Equipment (Six static compaction systems 
with loading mechanism, 18 detachable containers and eight Hook Loaders with Vehicle). 
The Work Order was issued for a total cost of ` 8.47 crore. The supplier supplied all the 
materials ( December 2017) as per order and the payments were  made accordingly 
(December 2017 to April 2018).  
After the completion of the supply order, the SCC, Indore assessed additional requirements 
for the same equipment and another work order amounting to ` 8.59 crore was issued to the 
same supplier on the basis of previous order, without resorting to tendering. There was no 
mention of any urgency in the documents relating to the grant of approval for work order.

5.1.6.4   Infructuous expenditure due to deficiencies in tendering process  
The SCC, Indore envisaged an intelligent transport management system for the public at an 
estimated cost of ` 40.00 crore. The system was to be installed at 30 places, and was to be 
replete with smart variable messages, reflective sign boards, cautionary boards, etc.  
Based on the tendering process, the L1 bidder was awarded the contract and a Work Order 
was accordingly issued for a contract amount of ` 40.56 crore (August 2019). The Contract 
also provided for depositing of Performance Guarantee in the form of Bank Guarantee by 
the selected bidder and the contractor accordingly deposited Bank Guarantee amounting to 
` 2.03 crore.  
The contractor accordingly started the work and upto March 2021, the payments of ` 23.38 
crore had been processed against the work done. The first running bill was paid in November 
2019. It was seen that the contractor thereafter failed to complete the work and the contract 
had to be terminated (July 2021). In this regard, Audit observed the following issues: 
• The Central Vigilance Commission’s Office Memorandum (December 2002) provides 
the eligibility criteria for award of work to a contractor after assessing pre-qualifications 
for the work which includes Average Annual Financial Turnover during the last three 
years and experience of the contractor having successfully completed similar works 
during previous seven years. It was seen that no such criteria for the assessment were 
fixed in the tender document to assess the capacity of the contractor to successfully 
execute the work. Thus, the SCC , Indore awarded the work order, on the basis of a 
deficient tendering process, to a contractor who was not competent to complete the 
work.  
• Consequently, the contractor could not complete the work and the contract was 
terminated (July 2021) under the clauses of the agreement. Thus, the failure of the SCC, 
Indore to adhere to a robust tendering process resulted in infructuous expenditure 
amounting to ` 23.38 crore. Further, the SCC has not penalised the contractor for failure 
to complete the work by encashing the Bank Guarantee amounting to ` 2.03 crore 
(submitted by the contractor before execution of work).  
GoMP stated that the matter is to be d ecided by the Honorable High Court. However, the 
fact remains that the contract was awarded to  a contractor which was not competent to 
complete the work , resulting in termination of the contract . The reply was silent about 
assessing per-qualification and n ot encashing the bank guarantee after termination of the 
contract.

5.1.7.1   Working of High-Powered Steering Committee  
As per Smart City Mission guidelines, there shall be a State level High Powered Steering 
Committee (HPSC) 18, which would steer the Mission Programme in its entirety. The key 
responsibilities of the HPSC are to provide guidance to the Mission and provide a State level 
platform for exchange of ideas pertaining to development of Smart Cities. The GoMP

could not ascertain the role of the HPSC and whether they performed any productive 
function with regard to providing guidance to the Mission.

will be established at the city level for all Smart Cities to advise and enable colla boration

inception.

5.2.1   Introduction  
Article 243W of the Constitution of India envisages that the Legislature of a State may, by 
law, endow the municipalities with powers and authority to enable them to function as 
institutions of self -government and such law may contain provisions for the devolution of 
powers and responsibilities upon municipalities. Further, as per A rticle 243X of the 
Constitution of India, the Legislature of a State may authorize a municipality to levy and 
collect such taxes, duties, tolls and fees. Section 133(1) (a)(b) of the Madhya Pradesh 
Municipal Corporation (MPMC) Act, 1956 and Section 129 1(a)(b) of the Madhya Pradesh 
Municipalities (MPM) Act, 1961 provide that the Corporation or Council may, by a 
resolution, at the time to final adoption of the budget estimates for the next financial year 
impose taxes or fees as specified and increase the rate of taxes or fees already imposed. The 
sources of own revenue of Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) are tax revenue 22 and non -tax 
revenue23. Being the predominant components of receipts, property tax and rent24 have been 
selected for the purpose of audit, under tax and non-tax revenue respectively. 
The Urban Development and Housing Department (UDHD), headed by the Principal

governance of all ULBs. The Directorate, Urban Administration and Development (UADD), 
functions as an interface between the State Government and the ULBs. The UADD is headed 
by the Commissioner who is assisted by nine Joint Directors 25 at Division level. 
Commissioner and Chief Municipal Officer are the executive head of the  corporations and 
other ULBs (Nagar Palika Parishads and Nagar Parishads) respectively.

5.2.5   Property Tax  
A tax payable by the owners of buildings and lands situated within the city with reference to 
gross Annual Letting Value30 (ALV), also referred as Taxable Property Value (TPV) of the 
buildings or land is called Property Tax 31 (PT). It shall be charged, levied and paid, at the 
rate not less than six per cent and not more than 10 per cent of the ALV32. Further, properties 
owned by the Central government are exempted under the MPMC Act, 1956 and the MPM 
Act, 1961, however Service Charge is leviable on such properties for services provided by 
ULBs. According ly, issue relating to the Service Charge has also been covered in this 
Paragraph along with the Property Tax. 
5.2.5.1   Non revision of the rates for determination of ALV/TPV  
Section 138 of the MPMC Act, 1956 and Section 126 of the MPM Act, 1961 provide that 
the ALV/TPV of any building or land shall be determined as per the resolution adopted by 
the Corporation/ Municipality. The Commissioner/ Chief Municipal Officer (CMO) shall 
prepare the draft resolution for the next financial year and submit it before Corporation or 
Council in the respective ULB before 31 December of each financial year. In case, the 
Corporation / Council fails to adopt the resolution by 31st March of each financial year then 
the draft resolution shall be presented to the Mayor/ Presid ent and the resolution approved 
by the Mayor/ President shall be deemed to be the finally adopted by the Corporation / 
Council.

in raising their PT revenue realising capabilities. Therefore, the objective of constitution of 
the Board could not be justified. 
On being pointed out in audit (June 2021), the  Deputy Director, UADD stated (September 
2021) that monitoring of work plan was being done by the Joint Directors at Division level, 
action was under consideration for recruitment of required staff and action regarding 
organisation of board meetings was un der process. Further, revenue staff were given 
continuous training by the training branch of the Directorate. No comment was offered by 
the Government in this regard. 
The replies of Deputy Director, UADD are not acceptable as compliance reports on the 
annual work plans were not available with the Department, therefore, it cannot be ascertained 
whether the activities of work plans were actually monitored. Further, the Board conducted 
only one online training programme and documentary evidence was not produce d to Audit 
to verify the veracity of the claim about continuous training given by the Directorate. 
5.2.5.8   Non-levy of PT on an open land/plots 
As per Section 132(1)(a) of the MPMC Act, 1956 and Section 127(1)(a) of the MPM Act, 
1961, PT was payable by the property owners on building or land located in ULB area on 
the basis of ALV/TPV.  
Audit observed PICs of two (NPP Tikamgarh and NP Bankhedi) ou t of 16 test -checked 
ULBs had passed a resolution for imposition of PT on open land/ plots. However, in 23 
cases, pertaining to these ULBs, PT of ` 0.12 crore was not imposed on open land/ plots. 
Further, NP Nalkheda did not pass any resolution for levy of PT on open land/ plots and PT 
was not levied on open land/plots, in this ULB.   
Thus, non-levy of PT on open land/plots resulted in non -levy of PT of ` 0.12 crore in the 
two ULBs (NPP Tikamgarh and NP Bankhedi), as detailed in Appendix 5.2.5.  
In reply, the Government stated (November 2022) that a resolution in this regard is pending 
with PIC in NPP Tikamgarh, while in case of NPs - Bankhedi and Nalkheda, no comment 
was offered. However, during the audit, CMO, NP, Bankhedi had stated (January 2022) that 
PT would be imposed on open land in future as per rules. CMO, NP, Nalkheda stated 
(September 2021) that the resolution could not be passed as PIC was in dissolved state since

that concrete effort was lacking in this regard. Further, the reply of CMO, NP, Nalkheda is

5.2.6   Rent 
As per Rule 2 (1) (q) MPMTIP Rule, 2016, the transfer of property means to confer the right 
to use of immovable property for certain period of time to one or more persons by the ULB 
under the condition as may be determined at premium and lease rent or as free hold. Further, 
Para 3(1) (2) of MPMTIP Rule, 2016 stipulates that ULB may grant lease of immovable 
property by inviting or without inviting tender.  
5.2.6.1   Premium of shops remained outstanding for recovery 
As per Rule 7 (2) of MPMTIP Rules, 2016, the whole amount of premium of shops should 
be remitted to the Government account within 120 days from the date of finalisation of the 
auction procedure. In the event of non -deposit of the amount of premium in the stipulated 
period, the Commissioner/ CMO shall notify that ‘the Lease is disqualified’ and tender shall 
be invited again. 
Audit observed (between June 2021 and January 2022) in six49 out of 16 test checked ULBs 
that against ` 22.87 crore, only ` 10.77 crore were deposited by the successful bidders even 
after the expiry from three to 875 days of the stipulated period of 120 days from the date of 
finalisation of the auction procedure. Thus, ` 12.10 crore against auctioned 94 shops were 
outstanding. Further, Audit also observed that the ULBs neither cancel led their allotments 
nor proceeded for the process of re -auction. Thus, due to inaction of the ULBs, amount of  
` 12.10 crore on account of the premium of 94 shops remained unrealised. The details of 
outstanding premium are given in Appendix 5.2.6. 
In reply, the Government stated (November 2022) that an amount of ` 1.33 crore had been 
recovered by three50 ULBs and recovery was in progress in remaining cases. Regarding NPP, 
Shajapur, it was stated that outstanding ` 43.00 lakh pertaining to 2020 -21 have been 
recovered. In the case of NN, Bhopal, it was stated that action was being taken under the 
MPMTIP Rules, 2016 and ` 61.08 crore had been recovered during 2021 -22. However, it 
was not informed that how much of this amount pertains to the period covered in audit, i.e., 
2018-19 to 2020-21. Further, in the case of NPP, Biaora, no comment was offered. However, 
during the audit, the CMO, NPP, Biaora had stated (August 2021) that Audit will be 
informed after taking necessary action. Further, progress of recovery wa s not informed to 
Audit by NPP, Biaora and reply of the Government regarding the amount recovered also 
needs further substantiation from records.

5.2.6. 2 (Arrear of rent) above. This indicated that the monitoring by the Directorate was not 
up to the desired level and needed further improvement. 
5.2.8   Conclusion 
As per the provision c ontained in MPMC Act, 1956 and MPM Act, 1961, the ULBs are 
empowered to self-govern by imposition of taxes or fees. Being the main source of revenue 
for ULBs, the increase in the PT revenue makes the ULB more self -dependent. However, 
during the period covered under Audit, it was seen that the ULBs did not recover ` 378.68 
crore as arrears of property tax, shop rent and premium of shops due to inaction of the ULBs 
in compliance of the laid-down procedure of recovery.  The instances of non -levy of PT of 
` 1.71 crore due on Board and Nigam office buildings had also been noticed. Besides, the 
Service Charge on the properties of Central Government had also not been levied. 
Irregularities were noticed related to acceptance of incomplete self -assessment returns 
without checking by competent authority. Thus, the accuracy of levy of PT could not be 
ensured. The functioning of the Property Tax Board was not as per the requirement of the 
13th Finance Commission recommendations. The above lapses indicated non -compliance 
with the provisions of Acts and Rules which impacted the revenue collection by the ULBs.

the Directorate of UADD:

ensure the correct computation of ALV of the Properties by putting all the details in

5.3   Water Supply Management in Urban Local Bodies 
 
5.3.1   Introduction 
The 74th Constitutional Amendment made the Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) responsible for 
the administration and maintenance of Water Supply within the municipal limits. The 
financial and administrative control of ULBs in the State rests with the Directorate of Urban 
Administration and Development (UAD), headed by the Commissioner, under the Urban 
Development and Housing Department (UDHD). At the Municipal Corporation level, the 
Commissioner is assisted by Superintending Engineer (Water Supply), Executive Engineer, 
Assistant Engineer (AE), Sub-Engineer and other staff to discharge their duties for smooth 
water supply. The Municipal Council is headed by the Chief Municipal Officer (CMO) and 
the senior most engineer in the Municipal Council is in-charge of Water Supply.  
5.3.2   Audit Objectives 
The Compliance Audit is aimed at assessing whether:  
• Sufficient water is available and supplied to the consumers as per laid down norms; 
and 
• Drinking water and services of appropriate quality are being supplied to the 
consumers, in all the selected ULBs. 
5.3.3         Audit Criteria 
Audit criteria were sourced from the following: 
• Madhya Pradesh Municipal Corporation Act, 1956 and Madhya Pradesh 
Municipalities Act, 1961; 
• Central Public Health and Environmental Engineering Organisation 57 (CPHEEO) 
Manuals on Water Supply and Treatment, 1999 and Manual on Operation and 
Maintenance (O&M) of Water Supply System, 2005; 
• State Water Policy, 2003; 
• Specifications for Drinking Water (IS10500:2012) issued by Bureau of Indian  
Standards; and 
• Handbook on Service Level Benchmarks published by Ministry of Urban 
Development (MoUD), Government of India.  
5.3.4   Audit Scope and Methodology 
The Audit was carried out during June and November 2021 covering three-year period from 
2018-19 to 2020-21. Audit involved scrutiny of records of three selected ULBs viz. Gwalior 
Municipal Corporation (GMCn), Jabalpur Municipal Corporation (JMCn) and Vidisha 
Municipal Council (VMC) along with joint physical verification with the ULB authoriti es.

to Urban Water Supply and Sanitation including Solid Waste Management in the country.

5.3.6   Non-preparation of operation and maintenance plan 
As per para 2.4.2 of CPHEEO (O & M) Manual 2005, a comprehensive operation and 
maintenance plan shall be prepared to cover all the facilities. It is the responsibility of 
operational management headed by the Superintending Engineer to prepare operation and 
maintenance plans. 
On being enquired about preparation of a comprehensive operation and maintenance plan, 
all the test-checked ULBs intimated (July 2021, September 2021 and November 2021) that 
operation and maintenance plan has not been prepared. JMCn and VMC also intimated (July 
2021 and November 2021) that whenever required, the maintenance works were done by the 
staff of their Water Supply wing. The GMCn intimated (September 2021) that the 
supervisory staff were assigned duties of operation and maintenance and check lists were 
prepared for that purpose. However, documents to verify the same were not produced to the 
Audit.  
In reply the Government stated (November 2022), in the case of GMCn that the 
comprehensive operation and maintenance plan had been prepared every year and a Cell had 
been set up for operation and maintenance of Water Supply System under P ublic Health 
Engineering Department. Presently the work has been assigned to a Contractor. However, 
the reply was not supported by any documentary evidence in this regard. The reply was silent 
about preparation of comprehensive operation and maintenance plan in JMCn and VMC. 
5.3.7   Assessment of quantity of water required and distribution of   water 
Para 2.2.8.1 of CPHEEO Manual on Water Supply and Treatment, 1999 provides that piped 
water supplies for communities should provide adequately for domestic needs, institutional 
needs, public purposes, and industrial and commercial uses, etc. Audit observed the 
following: 
5.3.7.1   Non-assessment of institutional demand for water 
Table 2.1 of para 2.2.8.3 of CPHEEO Manual on Water Supply and Treatment, 1999 had 
prescribed different norms for the assessment of water required by the institutions like

Hospitals (340 to 450 Litre  Per Capita per Day  (LPCD) per bed), Hostels and Boarding 
Schools/Colleges (135 LPCD), Schools/Colleges (45 LPCD), Restaurants (70 LPCD per 
seat), Cinema and Theatres (15 LPCD), etc.   
Thus, while assessing the demand of water the ULBs had to consider the institutional 
demand as well. Test-checked ULBs intimated (VMC – July 2021, GMCn – September 2021 
and JMCn – November 2021) that the actual need of water to institutions was not assessed 
by them.  
In reply, the Government stated (November 2022) that in case of JMCn, 15 per cent non-
domestic demand was added under the AMRUT Phase -1 whereas in DPR for Phase -2, 
provision for institutional deman d was made. In the case of VMC, it was stated that 
institutional demand was considered only on a demand basis because additional requirement 
without demand would only increase expenditure. While in the case of GMCn, it was stated 
that assessment for institutional demand was done under the AMRUT Project -1. Reply 
confirms that all three ULBs had not done assessments on the basis of actual number of 
existing institutions as per the provisions in aforesaid CPHEEO Manual. Further, in GMCn, 
the institutional demand covered State and Central Government Institutions only. 
5.3.7.2 Huge difference between quantity of water received and   distributed 
due to water losses 
Para 2.6.5 of CPHEEO O&M Manual of Water Supply System, 2005 states that there are 
considerable losses between water produced and distributed which leads to reduction in the 
income of the utility. The manual also suggested that water audit should be done to get fairly 
accurate figures of the water production, water assessed, losses both physical and revenue. 
Such an audit could lead the ULBs to prioritise actions required to reduce these losses.   
On being enquired all the test -checked ULBs intimated ( VMC – July 2021; GMCn – 
September 2021 and JMCn – November 2021) that they have not conducted any water audit. 
Audit also observed that the test-checked ULBs did not have a procedure for measuring the 
quantity of water received, filtered and distributed in their network due to which they were 
unable to quantify the water losses in their network. 
According to Section 2.1.4 of Handbook on Service Level Benchmarks published by 
Ministry of Urban Development (MoUD), Government of India , the extent of water 
produced which does not earn the utility any revenue was termed as Non -Revenue Water 
(NRW).

water to its full capacity and the whole water was supplied to the inhabitants in one supply 
period, revealed considerable loss of water in test checked ULBs as detailed below:

5.3.8.1   Quality of supplied water not ensured 
State Water Policy 2003 envisages that the quality of surface and ground w ater shall be 
tested on a regular basis by the concerned department. As per para 2.2.9 read with para 15.1 
of CPHEEO Water Supply and Treatment Manual, 1999 the objective of the Water Works 
Management is to ensure that the supplied water is palatable and free from undesirable taste 
and odour for which laboratories (labs) with adequate facilities and manned by qualified 
personnel are essential.  The aim of laboratory examination of water is to ensure that potable 
water conforming to the drinking water standa rd is supplied to consumers. Annexure -17.1 
(Job description) of CPHEEO O&M Manual of Water Supply System, 2005 envisages that 
the responsibility of the Middle/Operational Management (Deputy Assistant to the 
Executive Engineer) is to monitor alum dosage and  chlorine dosage. Mainly four types of 
tests were to be conducted in the laboratory, i.e., physical, chemical, bacteriological and 
biological analysis, so that it prevents adverse effects on the health of the population.  
Audit observed that only seven 59 out of the 31 parameters 60 were being tested in the 
Motijheel lab of GMCn. As the samples were not tested for ascertaining the values of the 
remaining parameters, the quality of water supplied was not ensured. Thus, adverse effects 
on the health of the population cannot be ruled out. 
The EE, Water Supply, GMCn intimated (September 2021) that all parameters were not 
tested during 2018-21, as facilities for checking those parameters were not developed in the 
lab. 
Audit also observed that during the period 2018 -21, GMCn had collected 8,373 samples 
from different locations of the city for ascertaining their physical (2,791 samples), chemical 
(2,132 samples), bacteriological (659 samples) and biological (2,791) parameters. Out of 
these, results of 56 samples of phys ical analysis, eight samples of chemical analysis  
(alkanity 3, hardness 5) and 158 samples of bacteriological analysis (Coliform (MPN61) 157, 
faecal coliform 1) were found adverse. 
In JMCn, only Lalpur Filtration Plant had the facility for checking all the  required 
parameters. Test results of city samples were made available only for the period 20 January 
2020 to 2 September 2020 for scrutiny. During this period 188 samples were taken from 
different locations of the city, out of these 22 samples (15 samples in physical, five samples 
in bacteriological and two samples in both parameters) were found adverse. Action taken on 
the adverse samples by the EEs of GMCn and JMCn was not ascertainable in absence of 
records to verify them.  
The water testing lab of VMC was not functional due to the non-availability of chemist there. 
As such there was no system for regular checking of water samples.

5.3.8.2   Supply of bore well water without testing 
As per a report of CGWB the quality of ground water has undergone a change to an extent 
that the use of such water could be hazardous. An increase in overall salinity of the ground 
water and/or presence of high concentrations of fluoride, nitrate, iron, arsenic, total hardness 
and few toxic metal ions have been noticed in large areas in several states of India. These 
can cause problems like stomach pain, digestive problems, kidney stones, jaundice, typhoid, 
liver, heart and pancreatic damage.  
During test-check of r ecords in the test -checked ULBs, it was observed that as of March 
2021, 2,199 bore wells in GMCn, 2,981 bore wells in JMCn and five bore wells in VMC 
supplied water in their jurisdiction without any quality testing.  
Audit also observed that in GMCn (Motijheel Water Testing Laboratory,) during the period 
from April 2018 and March 2021 and, JMCn (Lalpur Water Testing Laboratory) during the 
period 21 January 2020 and 4 September 2020 (period for which record was produced), had 
collected 75 water samples from borewell (57 by GMCn and 18 by JMCn) from different 
locations of their jurisdiction, on the basis of complaints from its inhabitants. Out of the 57 
samples of GMCn, 16 samples were such in which either turbidity or coliform or both 
turbidity and coliform w ere not as per permissible limits prescribed under IS10500:2012.  
All the 18 bore well samples taken by JMCn also contained non-acceptable ranges of various 
parameters. 
In reply, the Government stated (November 2022) that in JMCn, supplied bore well water is 
also used for purposes other than drinking. However, the reply is silent about regular testing 
in JMCn. As regards VMC, it was stated that testing is being done from time to time. Further 
the register relating to test results (for month August 2022) indicated that the testing is done 
after the issue raised in Audit. In the case of GMCn, it was stated that individual bore -well 
water was not being supplied to a particular lane. The bore-well water along with OHT water 
was supplied in Wards through the same  pipeline. The mixed water matches the quality 
parameter as prescribed in the CPHEEO Water Supply and Treatment Manual, 1999. 
However, the test results of water supplied from bore well was poor and both turbidity and

5.3.8.3   Irregularities in use of Coagulant 
Para 5.4.1.3 of CPHEEO O&M Manual of Water Supply System, 2005 states that the 
selection of proper type and amount of coagulant to be added to the water to be treated  is 
very important. Overdosing as well as underdosing of coagulant may lead to reduced solids 
removal efficiency. This condition may be corrected by carefully performing jar tests.  
The observations on the use of coagulant noticed in the test-checked ULBs are discussed in 
the paragraphs below: 
• Regular testing of samples not done  
Para 5.3.6 of CPHEEO Water Supply and Treatment Manual, 1999 provides that samples of 
raw and treated water will be taken at regular intervals for analysis. Further, in large 
waterworks having their own laboratory, sampling is to be done daily.  
Audit observed that Bhongadwar Filtration Plant (BFP) of JMCn did not have a laboratory 
of its own, thus, water samples from this plant were being tested in labs of other filtration 
plants situated at Jabalpur (i.e., Lalpur or Ranjhi). Verification of water sample testing 
records for the period 21 January 2020 to 4 September 2020 (period for which records were 
produced), revealed gap of one to 137 days between one test and the subsequent test. 
Motijheel Water Testing Laboratory of GMCn had its own lab, however scrutiny of records 
revealed a gap of two to four days between conduct of one test and subsequent test 
(Appendix-5.3.2). 
The EE, GMCn intimated (September 2021) that regular tests would be conducted in future. 
In reply, the Government stated (November 2022) regarding the issue in GMCn that quality 
of raw water for all the four water treatment plants was assessed regularly in the laboratory. 
But the fact remains that during the audit, there was a gap of two to four days between 
conduct of one test and subsequent test as per the records. Regarding the issue in JMCn, the 
reply was silent. However, during audit, the EE, Water Supply, JMCn intimated (November 
2021) that regular tests of water samples of BFP could not be done as they do not have their 
own laboratory.   
• Use of coagulant without jar test 
Para 5.4.1.4 of CPHEEO O&M Manual of Water Supply System, 2005 states that the jar test 
is still the most widely used method employed to evaluate the coagulation process and to aid 
the plant operator in optimising the coagulation, flocculation and clarification processes by 
using the correct doze of coagulant.   
Audit observed that the dosages of chemicals by BFP of JMCn and the filtration plant of 
VMC were not decided after conducting jar test. Thus, use of 2,56,885 kilogram (kg) alum, 
1,07,735 kg lime and 49,298 kg bleaching powder for water treatment by BFP during the 
period January 2019 and Mar ch 2021; and use of 28,693 alum bricks, 3,133.5 bags of 
bleaching powder and 2,421.5 bags and 2,080 kg of lime for water treatment during the years 
2018-19 and 2019-20 by VMC, was irregular.

The guideline issued (March 2017) by the UDHD stipulates that user charges for supply of 
water should be decided in such a manner that expenditure inc urred on operation and 
maintenance is recovered from the user charges. Further, GoMP gazette notification 
(September 2020) also envisages to determine the rates of user charges for water supply, in 
such a manner that annual expenditure incurred on water supply services are recovered cent 
per cent. The procedure of determination of rates is also prescribed in paragraph 4 of GoMP 
gazette notification (September 2020).  
Audit observed that compliance to the UDHD guideline and gazette notification was not 
being done by the test -checked ULBs, and user charges for use of water was levied at the 
ad-hoc rate of ` 150 per month by GMCn, ` 170 per month by JMCn and ` 100 per month 
by VMC. Water user charges levied on flat rate basis by the ULBs resulted in non -
compliance of the Government instructions and acted as a disincentive for consumers to 
conserve water. 
In reply, the Government stated (November 2022) that in JMCn, the user charges were fixed 
by the Municipal Corporation and sent to the Government for approval. But due to the 
Government's ban on implementing the new rate, the recovery was not done. In the case of 
VMC, expenditure statement of O&M was enclosed with the reply, but nothing was stated 
on the compliance to Gazette Notification ibid. In the case of GMCn, it was stated that the 
Municipal Corporation will follow the guideline for recovery of water user charge as per the 
procedure laid down in Gazette Notification. The Reply corroborates audit observation. 
5.3.9.2   Low recovery efficiency of water charges 
Section 225 of the MP Municipal Corporation Act, 1956 stipulates that the arrears of the 
water charges are to be recovered from consumers and in case of non -recovery the water 
connection should be disconnected. Further, the Madhya Pradesh Municipalities Act, 1961, 
Section 127 (1) (b) read with sections 164 and 165 provides that when any amount is declared 
to be recovered, the Chief Executive Officer may cause to be served upon the person liable 
for the payment, a notice of demand and that if such person does not pay the sum demanded 
in the notice, the amount may be recovered on the application of the Council to a Magistrate, 
and such Magistrate may order recovery by distress and sale of any movable property or 
attachment and sale of immovable property belonging to such person.

charges in test-checked ULBs is shown in Table-5.3.7.

Chapter V: Compliance Audit 
171 
 
5.3.10   Conclusion 
The test-checked ULBs had not conducted water audit for having fairly accurate figures of 
water production, water assessed, losses (both physical and revenue), due to which they were 
unable to assess the exact quantity of raw water received for filtration,  water filtered, water 
received at OHTs and water distributed to consumers. Estimation carried out by Audit 
considering the storage capacity of available OHTs and the schedule of Water Supply 
followed by the ULBs revealed NRW ranging from minimum 18 per ce nt (VMC) to 
maximum 78 per cent (GMCn).    
CHPEEO Manual on Water Supply and Treatment, 1999 prescribes the norm of providing 
135 LPCD water to all, but maximum achievement by the ULBs as assessed by Audit was 
35 LPCD (in 2020 -21) by GMCn; 98 LPCD (in 2018 -19) by JMCn and 100 LPCD  
(in 2018-19) by VMC. Test-checked ULBs had not ensured zoning in their water supply 
network for ensuring equal distribution of water to all.     
There was no program for detecting visible and non -visible leakages in the ULBs due to 
which considerable expenditure was incurred on operation and maintenance works of 
distribution lines.   
In the three ULBs, 2.98 lakh (47.76 per cent) households were still out of water connection 
network. Water meters were not installed at the premises of consumers.  As such water tax 
was being recovered on flat rate basis which did not act as a deterrent against water wastage. 
Test-checked ULBs were supplying water obtained from borewells, to its inhabitants without 
testing. Supply of bore well water wi thout testing, could be hazardous for public health. 
Cases of use of coagulant without ascertaining the required dose by jar test, non -use of 
coagulant due to exhaust of stock , improper storage  in the test -checked ULBs were also 
observed. Samples of silt/ mud accumulated in the tanks to be collected for biological 
analysis, at the time of cleaning of OHTs to observe the presence of snails and worms, were 
not done by the ULBs. Independent water quality testing conducted by Audit revealed that 
out of 46 sampl es, reports of 21 samples showed presence of faecal coliform against the 
prescribed zero count.

172 
 
5.3.11   Recommendations 
In view of above findings, the following recommendations are required to be implemented 
by the UAD: 
• Water audit may be conducted to ascertain the quantity of water filtered, water 
distributed, and losses both in physical and revenue terms.  
• A robust leakage control programme may be prepared and implemented to minimise 
the time that elapses between the occurrence of leaks and repairs thereof. 
• All households may be brought under the water connection network, water metering 
of all connections may be ensured, and water user charges levied accordingly.  
• Testing of samples of water extracted from borewell for s upply may be conducted 
invariably.

1 Chief Executive 
Officers of ZP/JP 
As per Madhya Pradesh Panchayat (Powers and Functions of Chief 
Executive Officer) Rules, 1995, 
• Supervision and control the officers and servant of the Panchayat; 
• Convene the meeting of Panchayat and Standing Committee and maintain 
proceeding thereof. 
• Custodian of all papers and documents connected with proceedings 
of meeting of Panchayat and its Standing Committees; 
• May call any documents information, return, statement or report from any 
officer holding office under t he Panchayat or from any other district office 
of any department. 
• shall supervise and control the execution of all activities of the Panchayat.  
• Initiate proceeding, civil or criminal on behalf of Panchayats. 
• prepare annual development plans and budget and ensure efficient execution 
of schemes included for all matters relating to the accounts of Panchayat. 
• The Chief Executive Officer shall also exercise all such powers and perform 
such other functions and duties as may be delegated to him by Panchayat or 
assigned by the Stale Government. 
2 Technical assistance 
and Execution 
• To prepare plans for execution of schemes/programme. 
•  Prepare estimates and issuance of technical sanctions. 
•  To execute the works as per sanctions by executing agencies i. e. GPs or 
other agencies.  
• Supervision and valuation of works.
